Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Jamal Rivera (CTO - NorthBay), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng)
Recording ID: FF-20260527-8932

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Redwood demo of the Optimize console savings calculator and runtime recommendations focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies. Marcus walks through console scenarios, cost model assumptions, and a sandbox plan. NorthBay raises questions about VPC/private deployment, data retention, and latency SLOs. Agreement to run a 2-day sandbox and exchange traffic histograms and benchmark scripts.

Topics (auto tags):
- Optimize console demo
- Savings calculator
- Batching parameters and concurrency
- Prefix / KV cache hit strategies
- Cost model assumptions and spreadsheet
- Private / VPC concerns, SOC 2

00:00 Elena Park: All right welcome everyone, thanks for carving out time. I am Elena from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, and with me is Marcus Li, our systems SE. Today we're going to step through the Optimize console savings calculator and a couple of batching + cache scenarios that map to the traffic you described in the doc.

00:28 Jamal Rivera: Hey folks thanks for doing this, we've been looking at ways to get inference costs under control before ramp. Budget target is to keep 95th p99 latency under 300ms and cost per active session to roughly $0.02 per session on average, maybe ambitious, but that's the ask.

00:55 Marcus Li: Great, thanks Jamal. Quick outline: first I'll show the console - the "Savings Calculator" panel, then a live run of the recommendations tab where Optimize proposes batch sizes, kv (we sometimes call it k-v) prefix caching TTLs and lookahead parameters. We'll walk through the assumptions in the cost model - token rates, model vram, concurrency - and then map to a proposed sandbox. Note: the console sometimes shows product name as Redwood Optima in older builds, ignore that artifact.

01:30 Priya Nair: Quick callout we are doing a mix of short chat sessions (~150 tokens) and longer context retrieval sessions (1.5k tokens) so the distribution is bimodal. We also store conversation history server-side so we can do session affinity if needed.

01:52 Marcus Li: Perfect that's the sort of distribution that benefits from prefix/KV caching for the short-form flows. If you have many short sessions with repeated prompts, even a 30-40% cache hit rate can yield big token-savings.

02:18 Liam O'Connor: On infra side, we're leaning on a VPC private deployment for compliance - we need to understand where KMS keys live and whether logs cross our boundary.

02:40 Elena Park: Good to note. We'll cover network and encryption briefly; Marcus will follow up with security docs. We have a SOC 2 + whitepaper and a network diagram we can share.

03:02 Marcus Li: Opening the console now - navigating to Optimize -> Savings Calculator. (screen share) The calculator takes three main inputs: traffic histogram (sessions per sec & token dist), target latency SLO, and model profile. For the demo I picked a moderate LLM profile (approx 30ms token cost on A100 equivalent) to keep numbers conservative.

03:34 Marcus Li: First scenario - chat-support (short sessions avg 150 tokens). We simulate concurrency 300 and target 200ms tail. Baseline (no cache, batch size 1) cost estimate: $1.00 per 1k responses. With a simple batching policy (batch size target 8, gather-time 12ms) we drop token cost ~18%. Add prefix cache with 40% hit rate - additional 28% less token consumption, combined savings about 42% vs baseline. Those numbers are rounded and depend on model compute profile.

04:10 Jamal Rivera: Wait, 42% combined - what's overlapping here? We don't want to double count tokens avoided by batching vs cache.

04:25 Marcus Li: Good point. Our estimator models batching reducing compute per-token overhead (amortized kernel launch + IO) while cache removes whole token generation steps for prefixed segments. We simulate the pipeline so overlap is accounted: cache hits reduce the token stream the runtime sees; remaining requests are batched. So the savings are multiplicative on the residual.

04:52 Priya Nair: Could you show the actual calculation sheet? I want to check the tokenization assumptions - we're on an open model so tokenization differs a bit.

05:06 Marcus Li: Sure. Linking to the shared workbook: https://drive.redwood/docs/NorthBay-cost-model (demo link). The sheet exposes tokenization rate, model throughput, average tokens per response, and an estimator for effective GPU-milliseconds per response. We also include sensitivity knobs: cache hit rate, batch target, concurrency, and session affinity.

05:40 Marcus Li: Switching to scenario two - long retrieval sessions (1.5k tokens). For long sessions, batching has less relative benefit unless you can batch generation across users; prefix cache helps for repeated prompts or shared context like a product description. Here we recommend a hybrid: KV cache for canonical document prefixes (TTL 24h), and session KV for per-user context with shorter TTL (10m) to save recent convo tokens.

06:12 Liam O'Connor: TTLs worry me from a compliance side - does Redwood persist KVs on our side or in our VPC? How's encryption?

06:26 Marcus Li: For private deployment, you can host the KV store inside your VPC; keys are managed by your KMS (we support AWS KMS/HSM integrations). For hosted mode we encrypt-at-rest with our KMS and can provide audit logs. We'll attach the security doc.

06:48 Elena Park: Note for procurement - we'll include a clear matrix: hosted vs dedicated vs private and where logs/keys live.

07:05 Marcus Li: Next I'll demo the Optimize "Recommendations" flow. It suggests a set of configs given your target SLO. (console click sounds) The recs show: batch target 6-10 for short chats, gather-time 8-15ms; prefix cache TTL 60s for ephemeral prompts, 24h for static doc prefixes; prefetch lookahead depth 3 tokens for streaming cases to warm KV. There's also an "autosuggest" slider labeled "cost-sensitivity" that moves recommendations toward lower latency (more conservative batching) or lower cost (higher batching / longer TTL).

07:45 Jamal Rivera: That slider—if we slide to lowest cost do we risk violating p99 latency?

07:55 Marcus Li: Yes the slider is a policy guardrail. The console runs a Monte Carlo sim across your supplied traffic histogram and gives an estimated p50/p90/p99 and token-cost delta. We add a confidence band. For your 300 concurrency/200ms p99 target, lowering cost aggressively bumped simulated p99 to 420ms in the worst-case bins, so we'd recommend a canary.

08:25 Priya Nair: Can we get the raw sim output? Numbers per bin?

08:33 Marcus Li: Yes, the console exports the simulation CSV. I'll attach the export after the call. It has columns: bin_id, concurrency, batch_size, observed_p99_ms, token_cost_usd.

08:52 (short crosstalk)

09:10 Marcus Li: Real-world tip: batch sizing is workload-sensitive. If you have many ultra short 1-2 token prompts, batching window often dominates latency, so we tune gather-time aggressively and rely more on cache. Conversely, for many mid-length responses, batching gives high leverage.

09:40 Jamal Rivera: Our session affinity is sticky - we pin users to pods. Does Redwood require session affinity for KV effectiveness?

09:50 Marcus Li: Not strictly. Prefetch and shared KV can be globally available across pods if you accept the network lookup cost. Session affinity reduces lookup hops and makes cold-starts cheaper. The console has an option to model session-local vs global KV access latency.

10:15 Liam O'Connor: What's the operational overhead - do we need to maintain separate KV infra?

10:23 Marcus Li: If you're on private deployment we recommend colocating a lightweight Redis cluster for KV; we provide operators and helm charts. For hosted, we manage KV and expose a TTL policy API.

10:40 Elena Park: Let's talk numbers we used for the demo baseline: model cost assumed $0.0008 per token of inference (compute amortized), batch overhead 0.00015 per request, and network overhead 0.00005. These are conservative. If your internal model throughput is different we'll swap.

11:05 Priya Nair: 0.0008 per token seems high given our quantized model runs. We can push lower if we bring our own quantized variant.

11:15 Marcus Li: Absolutely — that's why we recommend a quick benchmark. Marcus to Priya: I can share a simple harness that runs 1000 queries through your quantized image to estimate real per-token ms.

11:30 Marcus Li: Back to the console — here's the "What-if" toggles. I'll enable "prefetch lookahead" set to 2. That instructs runtime to fetch likely next KV entries during generation for streaming use-cases which reduces stall time on the first streamed tokens. In the sim that shaved 30-60ms p50 on streaming flows in our tests.

12:00 Jamal Rivera: Do we need extra GPU memory for lookahead/prefetch?

12:07 Marcus Li: Minimal; lookahead pulls KV into RAM or warms local caches. The dominant memory footprint is still the model KV cache itself. We also have quantization-friendly modes to trade memory for compute.

12:30 Priya Nair: How do rollouts work? If we change TTLs or batch params, can we canary?

12:38 Marcus Li: Yes - Optimize has rollout controls: you can canary to a percentage of traffic or route by user segment. If p99 increases above a threshold it auto-rolls back. We also show before/after cost deltas in the console during rollout.

13:05 Elena Park: Quick qualification: timeline? Jamal mentioned ramp. If you need production-scale in 6-8 weeks we should scope the sandbox and benchmarks to give a confident estimate.

13:22 Jamal Rivera: 6 weeks is ideal. We want a pilot on dedicated capacity after the sandbox if numbers look good.

13:34 Marcus Li: Noted. We'll propose a two-phase plan: 1) 48-hour sandbox in our hosted sandbox (or in your VPC if you prefer) with synthetic traffic; 2) 2-week dedicated pilot with committed capacity for live sampling.

13:50 Priya Nair: For the sandbox, can we bring our SAML auth and KMS keys?

13:58 Elena Park: For hosted sandbox we can federate via SAML and we support customer-managed KMS in dedicated/private deplo. For hosted sandbox we'll need your security team to sign a brief MOU; Marcus will share the checklist.

14:20 Marcus Li: Sharing a link to the sandbox signup + checklist: https://redwood.ai/sandbox-signup. Also, the cost-model workbook has a tab called "Assumptions" where you can plug in your tokenization and quantized perf.

14:45 Jamal Rivera: Can you give us a quick sanity-run of savings for our mixed workload?

15:00 Marcus Li: Sure, live calculation using the workbook numbers you sent earlier (Priya's sample histogram). Baseline monthly estimate at 1M sessions: $28k. With conservative batching + 35% cache hit across short sessions we get down to $17.5k — roughly 38% savings. If we push TTL and batching more aggressively and accept a small p99 bump, could see up to ~53% in an optimistic run.

15:35 Priya Nair: That range helps; procurement will want the worst-case and best-case bands.

15:45 Marcus Li: We'll export triple scenarios: conservative, recommended, aggressive. Each will have the sim CSV and expected p99.

16:00 Elena Park: Objections we typically see: 1) risk of regressions in output quality when using cached prefixes (particularly for prompts that condition on user-specific context), 2) additional engineering overhead to maintain KV keys, 3) data residency / audit concerns. Let's address them quickly.

16:20 Marcus Li: For quality regressions we tie caching to prompt set evals — the console can run a small batch eval where cached responses are compared to fresh generation; we show diffs and a similarity metric. If we detect divergence above threshold we flag it.

16:45 Priya Nair: I like the eval hooks. We already have a few prompt sets we use for e2e checks; we can hand those off.

16:55 Jamal Rivera: On residency: if we go private we want full control. What's the cost delta for private vs hosted?

17:06 Elena Park: Private has a platform fee + infra; per our standard commercial terms we'll provide a dedicated costing sheet. Generally customers trade up-front platform fee for control and lower unit compute cost at scale. We'll include ballpark numbers in the workbook.

17:26 Liam O'Connor: Anything around SSO and RBAC?

17:33 Elena Park: We support SAML/SCIM for SSO and fine-grained RBAC in the console. We'll provide an export of roles and permissions.

18:00 Marcus Li: Quick demo of an exported sim CSV — showing p50/p90/p99 columns. (brief silence as file loads) There are noisy bins where concurrency spikes push p99 above 300ms; those are where we recommend canarying or routing to a lower-latency variant.

18:35 Jamal Rivera: Lower-latency variant meaning smaller model or dedicated capacity?

18:45 Marcus Li: Could be either. The console supports model routing policies: route on cost (cheaper quantized model) or route on latency (dedicated high-priority pool). You can set fallback rules automatically.

19:05 Priya Nair: For our first pilot let's keep model consistent and experiment with batching and cache only.

19:12 Marcus Li: Sounds sensible. I'll note that in the plan.

19:20 (brief hold music sound, someone joins)

19:50 Marcus Li: Quick live change - I'll flip the "cost-sensitivity" slider to aggressive cost saving and show simulated impact. You can see token-cost estimate drops, but p99 upper band widens. Console annotates which traffic bins are at risk.

20:20 Jamal Rivera: If we see risk in a bin, can we route only those to dedicated nodes?

20:28 Marcus Li: Yep, policy supports routing by hash or by detected payload size. So long-form responses could preferentially hit dedicated nodes while short chats use shared pools with caching.

20:50 Priya Nair: What's the expected engineering time to implement KV within our app if we want session local KV?

21:00 Marcus Li: With our SDKs it's usually 2-3 days to add KV set/get hooks and TTL logic for a single service, plus 2-3 days of integration testing. We'll provide example code.

21:20 Elena Park: I'll capture the timeline in the next steps: we'll send the workbook, sandbox link, and an integration quickstart.

21:32 Marcus Li: One more note about metrics: in addition to token-cost, we surface "wasted compute" which is generated tokens that were immediately truncated by a follow-up prompt, that can be mitigated by early-stop heuristics and by caching common prefixes.

21:55 Jamal Rivera: Do you have any references or case studies where customers saw >40% savings?

22:05 Elena Park: Yes, we'll share a short case study (link) where a SaaS search company saw 45% reduction after combining prefix caching and better batching along with quantization. Link: https://redwood.ai/case-studies/search-savings

22:25 Priya Nair: Any limitations to batching in streaming responses?

22:33 Marcus Li: Streaming is trickier: you can still batch on a per-token round but gather windows must be tiny. We often recommend hybrid streaming: do small initial batch to satisfy first tokens, then enlarge batch for subsequent tokens, plus use lookahead/prefetch to smooth.

22:58 (background typing)

23:10 Marcus Li: Final section — proposed pilot plan (verbal):
- 48hr sandbox: run synthetic and replay traffic, collect p50/p90/p99 and token-cost.
- Validate caching strategies: prefix vs session KV with a few TTL experiments.
- Run regression evals on prompt sets to check quality.
- Deliver a summary report and recommended config for a 2-week dedicated pilot.

23:42 Jamal Rivera: That works. Any commercial terms to note? We prefer monthly reserved capacity for pilot.

23:52 Elena Park: We'll include a small reserved pilot offer in the proposal. Marcus will draft the technical appendix.

24:05 Priya Nair: A couple quick technical Qs: 1) Are cached entries keyed by tokenized prefix or raw prompt? 2) How do you handle tokenization mismatch across models?

24:20 Marcus Li: Great Qs. We key by canonicalized token sequence ID (internally normalized) but the console shows human readable canonicalization. Tokenization mismatch is handled by token-normalization layer; we also expose a "tokenizer ID" so you can match to your tokenizer. If you use a custom quantized model, we recommend sending a tokenizer sample to our onboarding so we align.

24:50 Liam O'Connor: For sandbox networking - do you need open ports inbound?

24:58 Marcus Li: For private sandbox within your VPC we'll use outbound-only egress to pull images and communicate over customers' private endpoints. We'll provide a short list of allowed egress endpoints.

25:20 (silence, notes)

25:40 Elena Park: We're approaching the last segment, let's do a quick recap and explicit next steps.

25:48 Elena Park: Recap: Marcus demoed the savings calculator and recommendations, we agreed on a 48hr sandbox, Marcus will send the cost-model workbook and benchmark script, Priya will share token distribution and SLOs, Redwood will share SOC2 and network checklist.

26:10 Jamal Rivera: That matches. Please include the worst-case and best-case scenarios in the workbook for procurement.

26:20 Marcus Li: Will do — conservative/recommended/aggressive scenarios with sim CSV exports.

26:30 Priya Nair: Also include a small eval-run where we replace cached responses with fresh generation and measure delta for a sample of 500 prompts.

26:44 Marcus Li: Noted — the console has an "eval diff" export; we'll run that during sandbox.

27:00 Elena Park: Any final questions?

27:05 Jamal Rivera: One more: competitor comparison — how are you different than just running an internal optimized runtime?

27:15 Marcus Li: Short answer: we provide an opinionated runtime with built-in cost telemetry, autoscaling, rollout policies and the Optimize console which stitches batching + caching + routing with sims and eval hooks. Build vs buy tradeoff: many teams can implement parts but not the integrated observability and automated rollouts. We'll include a short appendix that compares build vs buy.

27:40 Priya Nair: Great. That helps procurement.

27:50 Elena Park: OK last bits — Marcus, do you want to run through the files you'll send?

28:00 Marcus Li: I'll send: 1) NorthBay cost-model workbook (with baseline/rec/agg tabs), 2) sandbox signup + checklist link, 3) benchmark harness (github gist), 4) security & SOC2 whitepaper, 5) sample sim CSV. Links will be in an email and I'll post in the shared drive.

28:25 Jamal Rivera: Timeline again? If we get the workbook by Friday and run sandbox next week then review week after, that hits our 6-week ramp.

28:36 Elena Park: Yes, we'll aim for that.

28:42 Marcus Li: One tiny demo addendum — I toggled "aggressive cache TTL" to show an extreme scenario. Be warned: some prompts that rely on ephemeral user state can get stale if TTL too long. We advise tieing TTL to session ID when in doubt.

29:05 Priya Nair: Makes sense. We'll prepare prompt examples for the eval diff.

29:18 (brief pause)

29:30 Elena Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the attachments and action items. Marcus, anything else?

29:38 Marcus Li: No, that's it. I'll follow up with the exports and scripts.

29:45 Jamal Rivera: Appreciate it, looking forward to sandbox.
